newsitem.title: USA: Columbus City S.D., Ohio, GOs cut to A-plus - S&P.
newsitem.headline: Columbus City S.D., Ohio, GOs cut to A-plus - S&P.

text.p: NEW YORK, Sept 23 - Standard & Poor's Corp Monday said it lowered its rating on Columbus City School District, Ohio, $26.6 million G.O. bonds to single-A'-plus from double-A'-minus.
The downgrade is due to deterioration in the district's financial position over the past three years, resulting in increased short-term borrowing to balance operations.

The Columbus City School District encompasses about 67% of the city of Columbus (triple-A' G.O. rating). The city continues to enjoy strong growth through annexation of developing areas outside the school district, benefiting greatly from the expansion of the employment base through its municipal income tax. School district revenues consist mainly of property taxes (61% of total revenues) and state aid (36%). Tax base growth of the district has been flat over the past decade, averaging less than 2% a year since 1989. Ohio law precludes the district from capturing inflationary increase in tax revenue, leaving the district dependent on state aid increases in the absence of real property tax base growth.

Lower state aid due to declining enrollments and slow property tax revenue growth contributed to consecutive operating deficits totaling a combined $32 million in fiscals 1994 and 1995. The general fund balance totaled a negative $17.2 million on a GAAP basis at June 30, 1995. On a cash basis, the general fund balance totaled $6.9 million (2.0% of expenditures) after various accounting adjustments. Budget cuts totaling $12.7 million and a spending reserve borrowing of $13.6 million in short term notes, representing the use of the subsequent year's tax receipts, enabled the district to balance the fiscal 1996 budget. The ending general fund balance on a cash basis at June 30, 1996, totaled $8.6 million, or 2.3% of the district's $353 million operating budget.

Additional budget cuts of $28 million, including layoffs of 260 employees, and $14 million of spending reserve borrowing authority was necessary to balance the fiscal 1997 budget, which projected revenue growth of 4.2%. A 5.5 mill permanent property tax levy is on the November 1996 ballot, representing the district's first levy election since 1991. If passed, the levy is projected to generate about $36 million annually, which would allow the district to restore some previous budget cuts and eliminate the need for further spending reserve borrowing.

The outlook reflects the expectation that the district will manage operating budget pressures successfully and maintain positive financial results within the constraints of Ohio's school funding laws, Standard & Poor's said.
